rca_analyses_list.diagnosis: Frontend is attempting to connect to the Consul-style service name 'srv-search' but the Kubernetes Service is named 'search' (no 'srv-' prefix). This DNS/name mismatch prevents the frontend from resolving/reaching the search Service (which exposes port 8082).
rca_analyses_list.reasoning:
1) Frontend logs show the gRPC client target printed as 'srv-search.' (services/frontend logs: lines showing "get Grpc conn is :" followed by "srv-search.").
2) The Kubernetes Service for search in namespace test-hotel-reservation is named 'search' and exposes port 8082 (kubectl describe service search -n test-hotel-reservation shows Name: search, Port: 8082, Endpoints: 10.244.1.32:8082). 
3) The frontend Deployment has no explicit env var overriding the search host/port and the frontend reads Consul (log: "Read consul address: consul:8500"), indicating it expects Consul-registered names (e.g., 'srv-search'). Because the k8s Service DNS name is 'search' the frontend's 'srv-search' lookup will not match, causing the connection failure.

insights: Frontend calls five downstream services: reservation, search, profile, recommendation, user (from get_services_used_by).
Kubernetes Service 'search' exists in namespace test-hotel-reservation (ClusterIP 10.96.226.156) and exposes port 8082 with endpoint 10.244.1.32:8082 (from kubectl_describe).
Frontend Deployment runs a container exposing containerPort 5000 and has no explicit environment variable overriding downstream host/port (from kubectl_get).

Frontend pod logs show it reads Consul address 'consul:8500' and attempts gRPC connections using Consul-style names prefixed with 'srv-' (examples in logs: 'srv-search.', 'srv-profile.', 'srv-recommendation.', 'srv-user.', 'srv-reservation.').
Correlation of logs and Service description reveals a name mismatch: frontend is trying to reach 'srv-search' while the Kubernetes Service is named 'search' (no 'srv-' prefix).

Because the frontend uses the 'srv-<name>' Consul-style names and there is no matching Kubernetes Service name, the frontend cannot resolve/reach the search service despite the service and endpoints existing. This name/DNS mismatch is the root cause of the connectivity failure (confirmed hypothesis).

final_report.root_cause: The frontend is configured to use Consul-style service names with an 'srv-' prefix (e.g., 'srv-search') while the Kubernetes Service is named 'search' (no 'srv-' prefix). This DNS/name mismatch prevents the frontend from resolving/reaching the search Service, so gRPC connections fail with 'rpc error: code = Unavailable desc = there is no connection available'. The search backend itself is healthy and registered, so the failure is caused by the frontend's service-discovery/target naming configuration.
affected_resources: service discovery usage by frontend (Consul target names 'srv-*')
final_report.evidence_summary: 1) Frontend logs show it reads Consul ("Read consul address: consul:8500") and attempts gRPC connections using Consul-style names prefixed with 'srv-' (examples: 'srv-search.', 'srv-profile.', etc.). 2) 20 gRPC Unavailable traces show frontend->search failures with error 'there is no connection available'. 3) Kubernetes Service 'search' exists and exposes port 8082 (kubectl describe shows Endpoints: 10.244.1.32:8082). 4) The search backend pod (search-5c64c8f5bc-s99vl) is Running and Ready, logs show normal startup and 'Successfully registered in consul', and pod status shows ready=true and restartCount=0. Together these confirm the search backend is healthy but the frontend is attempting to contact a non-matching service name ('srv-search'), causing the connection failures.
final_report.investigation_summary: Priority weighting: priority #1 (backend health) was investigated first and ruled out — the search pod is Running/Ready, has no restarts, logged normal startup and registered in Consul, and Service endpoints are present. Priority #2 (connection/name check) showed the frontend is using Consul-style 'srv-<name>' targets while the Kubernetes Service name is 'search' (no 'srv-' prefix). Correlating frontend logs and the Service description established the causal link: name/DNS mismatch in the frontend's service-discovery configuration prevents resolving the correct target and causes repeated gRPC Unavailable errors. Given this conclusive evidence, no further investigations are required to identify the root cause.
